slides.title: Appendix A: Review of Smooth Manifolds
slides.notes: This appendix is the working memory for the rest of the book; nothing here is new, but everything must be available without hesitation. Treat the lecture as a check on language and notation: charts, smoothness, tangents, submanifolds, bundles, fields, covers. Whenever a Riemannian construction appears later, students should be able to point back to a slide here that explains why the construction makes sense.

slides.title: The Appendix as a Dependency Map
slides.notes: Use the artifact to orient the lecture: the chain runs from topological preliminaries through smooth maps and tangents into submanifolds, bundles, and fields. Ask students to predict where covering maps belong on the diagram before you name the location. The point is to give them a mental index card so that later chapter dependencies feel like motion along edges instead of leaps between unrelated boxes.

slides.title: Topological Preliminaries: What Makes a Manifold
slides.notes: Three conditions show up in every definition of a manifold and each one earns its place. Hausdorff lets us separate points and trust limits, second countability buys partitions of unity which we will need to glue local objects, and local homeomorphism to Euclidean space gives the charts that turn topology into calculus. The line with two origins is the standard cautionary example; mention it so students remember why the Hausdorff hypothesis is non-decorative.

slides.title: Smooth Structure: Compatible Charts and Atlases
slides.notes: The smooth structure does not live on the manifold; it lives in the transitions between charts. Two charts are compatible exactly when their composition through the overlap is smooth as a map between open sets of Euclidean space. Stress that we take the maximal atlas so that two different starting atlases that agree on overlaps define the same smooth manifold; this removes a layer of arbitrary choice that students often worry about.

slides.title: Smooth Maps and Diffeomorphisms
slides.notes: The definition of a smooth map is engineered so the check reduces to ordinary multivariable calculus inside Euclidean space. Once chart independence is justified, smoothness becomes a local computation. Highlight that diffeomorphism is the right equivalence relation for smooth manifolds, just as homeomorphism is for topological spaces; later, the Riemannian setting will refine this further with isometries.

slides.title: Tangent Vectors: Derivations at a Point
slides.notes: Tangent vectors can be introduced as equivalence classes of curves, as derivations on smooth functions, or as columns of numbers in a chart. The derivations definition is the cleanest because it lives intrinsically on the manifold, but students should be comfortable converting between the three pictures fluently. The basis induced by a chart is the workhorse for computations and connects every later Riemannian formula back to ordinary partial derivatives.

slides.title: Submanifolds: Immersions, Embeddings, Submersions
slides.notes: All three submanifold notions are captured by the rank of the differential, which is the single piece of data students should learn to read first. Immersions allow tangent injection but tolerate global pathology, embeddings add the right topology, and submersions are responsible for the cut-out picture of level sets. The sphere example anchors the regular value theorem in a familiar object so the abstract statement does not float free of geometry.

slides.title: Vector Bundles: Smoothly Varying Fibers
slides.notes: A vector bundle packages a family of vector spaces over a manifold so that fibers vary smoothly. The local triviality condition is what allows local computations to behave like ordinary linear algebra, while the absence of a global trivialization is what produces nontrivial geometry. The tangent bundle is the canonical example to keep in mind because every Riemannian construction we meet later is either a tensor bundle built from TM or a section of one.

slides.title: Vector Fields, Flows, and Covering Maps
slides.notes: Two constructions close out the appendix: vector fields with their flows, and covering maps. The flow theorem promotes a vector field into a one-parameter family of partial diffeomorphisms, and the Lie bracket then measures whether two flows commute. Covering maps come back when we discuss completeness and universal covers in Riemannian geometry; the evenly covered neighborhood condition is the precise reason geodesics lift uniquely once a starting point is chosen.

slides.title: What This Appendix Supplies Later
slides.notes: Close by tying every later chapter back to this scaffolding. Charts give us computations, bundles host every Riemannian object we will study, and vector fields with their flows drive geodesics and isometric symmetries. Send students away with the diagnostic habit of asking which chart, which bundle, and which smooth map applies before they attempt any specific computation.
